name: Axolotl
teaser: A Mexican salamander that never grows up — keeping its gills, fins, and baby face for life, and regrowing lost limbs, hearts, and even parts of its brain. It was sacred to the Aztecs and is now nearly extinct in the wild.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the axolotl stays in its larval form (neoteny) and regenerates limbs, spinal cord, and heart tissue without scarring. Write why scientists study it for human medicine and why it is endangered in its only home, Lake Xochimilco.

name: Tardigrade (Water Bear)
teaser: A microscopic eight-legged animal that can survive boiling, freezing, the vacuum of space, and years without water by shriveling into a glassy tun. They live in moss and gutters everywhere — the toughest animal on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how tardigrades enter cryptobiosis — drying into a tun and slowing metabolism to almost nothing — then revive with water. Write the extremes they survived on the outside of spacecraft, and how their DNA repair works.

name: Immortal Jellyfish
teaser: Turritopsis dohrnii can reverse its own aging — when stressed or old, it folds back into a polyp and starts its life cycle again, potentially forever. The only known animal that cheats death.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Turritopsis dohrnii transdifferentiates its cells to return from medusa to polyp. Write the steps of the reversal and what it could mean for aging research — and why it is not truly immortal in practice.

name: Mantis Shrimp
teaser: A crustacean with punches faster than a bullet, eyes that see twelve color channels (we see three), and claws that can crack aquarium glass. Its strike creates a flash of heat as hot as the sun's surface — underwater.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the mantis shrimp's two claw types (smashers and spearers), its cavitation-bubble punches, and its twelve-photoreceptor eyes. Write how its eyes process color differently from human eyes and why the strike is so powerful.

name: Dumbo Octopus
teaser: A deep-sea octopus with ear-like fins that flap like a cartoon elephant's, hovering over the abyssal plain at depths where sunlight never reaches. It is one of the deepest-living octopuses ever filmed.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch footage of the dumbo octopus swimming with its ear fins and study how it lives on the abyssal floor. Write how deep it lives, what it eats, and how its fins help it glide without jet propulsion.

name: Goblin Shark
teaser: A living fossil shark with a translucent snout and jaws that shoot forward like a spring-loaded trap to grab prey in the deep. It is so rare that most people only know it from a single famous photograph.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the goblin shark extends its jaws at high speed to snatch prey. Write why its pinkish skin and long snout suit the deep sea, and how the 'living fossil' label applies to its ancient lineage.

name: Okapi
teaser: A striped forest animal that looks like a zebra-horse hybrid but is the giraffe's only living relative — with a long blue-black tongue and a neck shorter than its cousin's. It was unknown to science until 1901, hidden in the Congo's rainforest.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why the okapi is classified with giraffes despite its stripes, and how it uses its prehensile tongue. Write how it was discovered late, why it is endangered, and what the Congo Basin's forest means to it.

name: Saola
teaser: Called the 'Asian unicorn,' the saola is a forest antelope discovered in 1992 from antlers in a hunter's home — and still never photographed wild until 2013. It lives in the mountains of Vietnam and Laos, and scientists know almost nothing about it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the saola was discovered from horns and how it was finally filmed. Write why it is critically endangered, how snares threaten it, and what conservationists are doing to save a species almost no one has seen.

name: Quokka
teaser: A small wallaby on Rottnest Island, Australia, famous for its seemingly permanent smile — the 'happiest animal in the world.' It is fearless around humans and has become a selfie icon, though it is a real marsupial with a pouch and a tough life.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why quokkas look like they smile (a natural facial structure) and why they are unafraid of people. Write how Rottnest's island environment shaped them, how they survive drought, and why feeding them is forbidden.

name: Aye-Aye
teaser: A lemur with a long, thin middle finger that taps wood like a drum to find grubs, then hooks them out — the only primate using echolocation-style tapping. In Madagascar it was feared as an omen and killed on sight.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the aye-aye uses percussive foraging — tapping branches to hear hollow chambers — and its elongated finger for extracting larvae. Write how this niche works and how superstition once threatened the species.

name: Fennec Fox
teaser: The smallest wild fox in the world, with ears as big as its body that radiate heat and hear prey moving underground in the Sahara. Its sandy coat reflects sunlight and its paws are furry like snowshoes on hot sand.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the fennec fox's huge ears keep it cool and detect prey beneath the sand. Write its other desert adaptations — pale fur, furry feet, water-efficient kidneys — and how it lives in family burrows.

name: Maned Wolf
teaser: A long-legged fox-like canid from South American grasslands that looks like a fox on stilts — and is neither fox nor wolf. It walks like a deer, barks like a dog, and marks territory with a smell like hops.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn why the maned wolf has such long legs (to see over tall grass) and why it is in its own genus. Write about its diet of fruit and small animals, its distinctive urine odor, and its solitary lifestyle.

name: Three-Toed Sloth
teaser: The slowest mammal on Earth, moving about 40 meters a day, sleeping 15 hours, and descending from the trees about once a week to poop. Algae grow in its fur, giving it a greenish camouflage — and a whole ecosystem rides on its back.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how sloths' slow metabolism, low body temperature, and algae-covered fur suit a life of hanging upside down. Write about their weekly ground visit, why they swim surprisingly well, and how moths live in their fur.

name: Narwhal
teaser: The 'unicorn of the sea' — an Arctic whale with a spiraled tusk that is actually an elongated tooth, up to 3 meters long, with millions of nerve endings. No one fully agrees what the tusk is for.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn about the narwhal's tusk — a tooth with sensory nerves, possibly used for sensing, display, or sparring. Write how narwhals dive deep for fish under sea ice and how climate change affects their Arctic habitat.

name: Beluga Whale
teaser: The 'canary of the sea' — a white, melon-headed whale that sings, clicks, and chirps with a huge range of sounds and a flexible face that seems to smile. It can even mimic human speech.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to beluga calls and learn how the melon organ focuses their echolocation. Write why they are so vocal, how they navigate under Arctic ice, and how a beluga once reportedly imitated human words.

name: Vampire Squid
teaser: Not a vampire and not a squid, but a deep-sea cephalopod that lives in the oxygen-starved zone where almost nothing else survives. When threatened, it turns itself inside out like a spiky cloak — 'vampire' only in name.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the vampire squid survives in the oxygen minimum zone, using its blue blood and low metabolism. Write how it wraps its arms into a cloak when alarmed and how it feeds on marine snow instead of blood.

name: Pistol Shrimp
teaser: A tiny shrimp that snaps its claw so fast it fires a bubble that collapses with a shockwave as hot as the sun's surface — the loudest sound in the ocean, loud enough to stun fish. The snap also makes a flash of light.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the pistol shrimp's claw snap creates a cavitation bubble that collapses into a shockwave and sonoluminescence flash. Write how this stuns prey, why it is so loud, and how snapping shrimp colonies can interfere with sonar.

name: Archerfish
teaser: A fish that shoots down insects with a jet of water — calculating the refraction of light at the water's surface to hit prey above the surface. It can even learn to distinguish human faces.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how archerfish adjust their aim for light refraction and gravity to knock insects into the water. Write about their predictive water jets, their intelligence tests, and how they snap up the prey before rivals do.

name: Cleaner Wrasse
teaser: A tiny fish that runs an underwater car wash: larger fish line up at 'cleaning stations' to have parasites and dead skin picked off — and the wrasse even eats the mucus, keeping mouths open for inspection. Predators wait their turn.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how cleaner wrasse remove parasites and how client fish remember and return to reliable cleaners. Write about the mutualism, the 'cheating' cleaners that bite mucus instead, and how this behavior was studied on reefs.

name: Leafcutter Ants
teaser: Ants that cut leaves and carry them underground — but they do not eat the leaves. They feed them to a fungus garden, and the fungus feeds them: one of the oldest farming relationships on Earth, 50 million years old.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how leafcutter ants cultivate fungus on cut leaves in vast underground chambers. Write the full symbiosis — ant, fungus, and the bacteria that protect the fungus — and how a single colony can strip a whole tree overnight.

name: Army Ants
teaser: Nomadic ants with no permanent home — millions march in a swarm that clears the forest floor of insects, and they bivouac by linking their own bodies into a living nest. Their raids send wildlife fleeing.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how army ants form living bridges and bivouacs, and how their swarm raids flush out prey. Write how they cycle between nomadic and stationary phases, and which birds follow their raids to catch fleeing insects.

name: Bombardier Beetle
teaser: A beetle that defends itself by firing a boiling, explosive spray of chemicals from its rear — combining hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinone in a reaction chamber at 100°C, aimed like a turret with a 270° range.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the bombardier beetle mixes chemicals in a special chamber and ejects the hot spray as a pulsed jet. Write how the reaction is controlled, how it deters predators, and how its mechanism has inspired engineering.

name: Dung Beetle
teaser: A beetle that navigates by the Milky Way — rolling balls of dung in a straight line using the stars and the polarized light of the sun. The strongest animal relative to its size, some species push balls 1,000 times their own weight.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how dung beetles roll dung balls and navigate by the Milky Way's band of light. Write about their strength, how they use celestial cues, and the ecological role they play by burying dung.

name: Monarch Migration
teaser: A butterfly weighing half a gram that flies up to 4,800 kilometers to Mexican mountaintops it has never seen — great-great-grandchildren of the ones that left the previous year. Millions gather in trees so thick they bend branches.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how monarchs navigate to Mexico using the sun and a magnetic compass, and how multiple generations complete a single round trip. Write why they cluster in oyamel forests, and how milkweed loss affects them.

name: Snowflake Obsidian
teaser: A black volcanic glass flecked with white 'snowflakes' — crystals of the mineral cristobalite that formed as the molten glass cooled. Every flake is a frozen moment of a volcano's final hours.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how snowflake obsidian forms when lava cools so fast it becomes glass, then slowly grows white cristobalite spherulites. Write why the 'snowflakes' are round, where it is found, and how it has been used for tools and jewelry.

name: Aurora Sounds
teaser: For centuries, northern peoples reported hearing the aurora — faint crackles and whispers as the lights danced. Scientists long dismissed it, but recordings now capture aurora-related sounds: static-like crackles tied to magnetic storms.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how researchers finally recorded aurora-related hisses and crackles near the ground. Write the leading theory — electric discharge or charge buildup in the air — and why the sounds were once called a myth.
